body:
Why storage matters for solar energy

Solar radiation changes throughout the day and falls to essentially zero after sunset. Electricity demand and heat demand, however, may continue after sunlight is no longer available.

Energy storage separates the time when solar energy is collected from the time when it is used. The form of storage depends on the technology: a photovoltaic system can store electricity in a battery, while a solar thermal system can store heat in water or another thermal storage material.

Thermal energy storage (TES) means storing energy as heat, or through another thermal process, for use at a later time. In conventional CSP applications, stored heat can later be used to generate electricity.

Thermal storage in household solar heating

The simplest example is an insulated hot-water tank connected to a solar water heater. Sunlight heats water during the day, and the tank retains useful heat for later household or institutional use.

Insulation reduces heat loss but does not eliminate it. If stored heat is exhausted or water temperature falls below the required level, additional heating may be necessary.

Thermal storage in CSP plants

Many concentrating solar thermal systems can be combined with high-temperature storage. Molten salt is an important example of a medium used to store sensible heat, meaning energy stored through a rise in the temperature of a material.

A common conceptual arrangement uses a relatively cool storage tank and a hot storage tank.

  1. Charging: Solar heat collected at the receiver increases the temperature of the heat-transfer or storage medium.
  2. Storage: The heated medium is held in an insulated hot tank.
  3. Discharging: When electricity or process heat is required, the stored hot medium transfers heat to a working fluid or industrial process.
  4. Return: The cooled storage medium returns to the lower-temperature tank and can be heated again when solar energy is available.

Some designs use the same fluid to collect and store heat. Others transfer heat between a collector fluid and a different storage material. The essential principle is the same: solar energy is captured as heat and retained for later use.

What dispatchable solar thermal power means

An electricity source is described as dispatchable when its power output can be controlled and supplied according to system requirements within the limits of its available energy and equipment.

CSP with sufficient thermal storage can continue generating electricity for a period after sunset or during interruptions in direct sunlight. This gives it more control over the timing of generation than a solar system without storage.

Thermal storage does not provide unlimited energy. Its usable duration depends on the amount of heat stored, the temperature range, heat losses and the rate at which energy is withdrawn. A CSP plant with thermal storage is not necessarily capable of supplying electricity continuously under all weather conditions.

Thermal storage and batteries are different

FeaturePV with batteryCSP with thermal storage
Initial solar conversionSunlight directly into electricitySunlight into concentrated heat
Stored energyElectrochemical energy in a batteryThermal energy in a heated medium
Later electricity supplyBattery discharges through suitable electrical equipmentStored heat operates a power-generation process
Typical storage mediumRechargeable batteryMolten salt or another heat-storage material

Benefits and limitations of solar thermal power

Important benefits include use of renewable sunlight, the ability to provide direct heat for suitable industrial purposes and the possibility of storing thermal energy before conversion into electricity.

Important limitations include:

  • Dependence on direct sunlight: Conventional CSP loses much of its useful solar input in strongly cloudy or hazy conditions.
  • Land and site requirements: Large mirror fields require suitable open areas and space for associated equipment.
  • Heat losses: Receivers, pipes, tanks and heat-conversion equipment cannot retain or transfer all energy without loss.
  • Water requirements: Certain steam-cycle and cooling arrangements use water, and water may also be needed for cleaning mirrors. Requirements vary with the technology and cooling method.
  • Complexity: Mirrors, tracking equipment, receivers, heat-transfer systems and generators require maintenance.
  • Variable supply: Storage and other arrangements can reduce the effect of solar variability, but they cannot remove every operating constraint.

PV systems may use battery storage, while ordinary solar water heaters and CSP plants may use thermal storage, but storage does not change their basic solar conversion principles. PV produces electricity directly; non-concentrating collectors mainly produce heat; CSP concentrates sunlight to obtain high-temperature heat.

Prelims focus

  • Thermal energy storage retains heat for later use.
  • An insulated hot-water tank is a simple form of solar thermal storage.
  • Molten salt can store high-temperature heat in CSP systems.
  • Stored CSP heat can be used to operate a generator after sunset.
  • Battery storage and thermal storage retain energy in different forms.
  • Trap: Thermal storage can extend generation beyond sunshine hours, but it does not guarantee unlimited or continuous electricity production.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, Thermal Storage System Concentrating Solar-Thermal Power Basics, sections Two-Tank Direct System and Two-Tank Indirect System, and Solar Thermal Energy Storage and Heat Transfer Media, consulted 16 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, Concentrating Solar-Thermal Power Basics, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Solar Thermal Storage, Dispatchable Power and Practical Constraints

body:
Geographical distribution of the solar resource in India

India receives substantial solar radiation across many regions because of its geographical location and generally favourable sunlight conditions. However, the solar resource varies significantly with season, cloud cover, local climate, atmospheric dust and the nature of the terrain.

The relatively dry regions of Rajasthan and Gujarat offer favourable conditions for many solar energy applications. Their importance is connected with substantial sunshine and the availability of suitable sites in some areas. Western India's solar potential does not mean that every location has equal irradiation or that electricity generation is constant throughout the year.

The monsoon is an important consideration. Increased cloudiness can reduce direct sunlight, while scattered radiation may still reach photovoltaic panels. The balance between direct and diffuse sunlight helps determine the suitability of different technologies.

Matching solar technology to the resource

Solar PV and CSP use the same original energy source, but the suitability of a site depends on how each technology captures sunlight.

  • Photovoltaic systems: Use direct and diffuse sunlight. Their generation depends on the radiation incident on the modules, module performance, orientation and operating conditions.
  • Non-concentrating solar thermal systems: Collect sunlight as heat. Solar water heaters and dryers can make use of available solar radiation without the mirror concentration used in CSP.
  • Concentrated solar power: Requires a particularly favourable direct-beam resource because its mirrors concentrate sunlight onto receivers.

Other practical considerations include suitable land or rooftop space, shading, nearby electricity demand, access to the grid and, for some applications, availability of water.

Important solar energy locations in Gujarat

Charanka Solar Park, Patan district

Charanka Solar Park, also known as Gujarat Solar Park, is situated at Charanka village in Santalpur taluka of Patan district. It is an example of large-scale, ground-mounted solar electricity development.

The park illustrates how multiple solar installations can be developed within an area supported by shared infrastructure. Its location is an important Gujarat geography fact: Charanka is in Patan district.

Khavda solar development, Kachchh district

Khavda, in Kachchh district, is another important location associated with large solar energy development.

A Ministry of Power press release dated 15 March 2024 announced that NHPC had secured a bid to develop a 200 MW solar PV project at a renewable energy park in Khavda. The figure describes the project announced in that release, not the total capacity of all solar projects at Khavda. The 2024 announcement alone does not establish the project's commissioning status on 16 November 2026.

Modhera solar-powered village, Mehsana district

Modhera is situated in Mehsana district. On 9 October 2022, it was officially declared India's first 24x7 solar-powered village.

The reported project combined a ground-mounted solar power plant with more than 1,300 rooftop solar systems on residential and government buildings, integrated with a battery energy storage system (BESS).

The designation highlights an integrated solar electricity and storage arrangement. It does not mean that photovoltaic cells generate electricity at night. It also should not be interpreted, without additional evidence, as proof that the village operates permanently without any interaction with the wider electricity network.

The Modhera details refer to the official declaration and project description of 9 October 2022. The Khavda project detail refers to a development announcement of 15 March 2024. These are dated facts, not claims about every installation's operating status or capacity as of 16 November 2026.

Elementary applications relevant to India

Solar energy can serve different needs without requiring every application to generate electricity.

ApplicationTechnologyUseful output
Rooftop electricityPhotovoltaic modulesElectrical energy
Solar irrigation pumpPhotovoltaic system with motor and control equipmentElectrical power for pumping
Solar street lightingPhotovoltaic system, often with battery storageElectrical energy for lighting
Household hot waterSolar thermal collectorHeat transferred to water
Crop dryingSolar thermal dryerHeat for moisture removal
Solar thermal power plantConcentrated solar powerHeat used for electricity generation

Putting the technologies together

The essential distinction is the first useful energy form produced from sunlight. Photovoltaic cells produce electrical energy directly. Solar thermal collectors produce heat for immediate use or storage. CSP systems concentrate sunlight to obtain higher-temperature heat, which can drive a power-generation process or serve a suitable industrial application.

Storage is a separate decision. Batteries may accompany photovoltaic systems, hot-water tanks may accompany household solar thermal collectors, and thermal storage may accompany CSP plants. None of these storage methods changes the underlying conversion mechanism.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat and Rajasthan are important western Indian regions with favourable solar resources.
  • Charanka Solar Park is located in Santalpur taluka, Patan district, Gujarat.
  • Khavda is associated with solar development in Kachchh district.
  • Modhera is in Mehsana district and was declared India's first 24x7 solar-powered village on 9 October 2022.
  • The Modhera project description included more than 1,300 rooftop systems and battery energy storage.
  • Trap: Solar-powered supply after sunset depends on storage or another supply arrangement; photovoltaic panels themselves require light to generate useful power.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, p. 82; Gujarat Power Corporation Limited, Annual Report 2022–2023, section Gujarat Solar Park; Gujarat Power Corporation Limited, tender document GPCL/PD/2023-24/02 dated 10 June 2024, annexure on Charanka location; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Power, NHPC to Develop 200 MW Solar Power Project at Khavda, 15 March 2024; Press Information Bureau, Prime Minister's Office, declaration of Modhera as India's first 24x7 solar-powered village, 9 October 2022; U.S. Department of Energy, Solar Radiation Basics and Concentrating Solar-Thermal Power Basics, consulted 16 November 2026.]
